title: Looking for Faults Before Cleaning a Raw File
learning_objective: Inspect a raw export for data-quality faults before writing any cleaning code, and rank which faults are dangerous because they fail silently versus loudly.
description_for_ai: Before writing a single line of cleaning code, a raw file should be scrolled and read, noting every fault visible by eye: a date column left-aligned (meaning Excel/the tool is treating it as text, not real dates), multiple date shapes coexisting in one column (e.g. 2026-07-14, 03/08/2026, 07-22-2026, 9 Sep 2026, 15.08.2026), a currency column stored as text because of a symbol and thousands separators (e.g. ₦45,320), a text column with an invisible trailing space making some cells sit slightly further right, and an identifier column using two different formats for the same value (e.g. LAG-07 and LAG07). Faults are not equally dangerous: a value like a naira sign breaks loudly the moment arithmetic is attempted on it, so it is caught immediately; an ambiguous date format like 03/08/2026 breaks silently, because both readings (3 August or 8 March) are valid dates, so nothing errors and roughly a third of a dataset's dates can silently move to the wrong month with the output still looking completely normal.
common_mistakes_for_ai: Jumping straight into writing cleaning code without first scrolling and reading the raw file to catalogue what is actually wrong. Treating every visible fault as equally risky, rather than distinguishing loud failures (which self-report via an error) from silent ones (which produce a plausible but wrong result). Assuming a mixed-format date column is safe because every individual value parses successfully - successful parsing does not mean correct parsing when the format is ambiguous. Missing an inconsistent identifier format (e.g. LAG-07 vs LAG07) because it looks like a minor cosmetic difference rather than a join-breaking mismatch.
example_code_for_ai:
# Faults found by inspection, before writing any code (SwiftRoute Q3 export):
# - date column left-aligned -> stored as text, not real dates
# - five different date shapes present in the same column
# - fee_naira reads "₦45,320" -> text, due to symbol + comma
# - rider_name has inconsistent leading/trailing spacing
# - route_code shows both "LAG-07" and "LAG07"
# Most dangerous: the mixed date formats - they fail silently, not loudly.

title: Using an AI Assistant to Describe Faults, Then Checking Its Counts
learning_objective: Prompt an AI assistant to list data-quality problems in a file and explain why its counts of specific problems (e.g. duplicates) must still be verified directly against the file rather than trusted as reported.
description_for_ai: An AI assistant given a raw file and asked to list data-quality problems reliably describes what is visible in a sample of rows - it will typically catch the mixed date formats and the currency-as-text problem, because those are visible in almost any sample. It is unreliable at counting exactly how many rows are affected by a specific problem (e.g. exact duplicate delivery IDs), because it is reasoning about a sample of the file, not scanning the full column the way code does. The correct workflow is to ask the assistant to describe qualitatively, then independently verify any quantitative claim (a count, a total, a percentage) by actually running code or a formula against the full file. Description from an AI assistant can be trusted as a starting point for investigation; counts from an AI assistant must always be checked, never accepted as-is.
common_mistakes_for_ai: Accepting a specific count reported by an AI assistant (e.g. 'there are about 30 duplicates') as fact without independently checking it against the actual file. Assuming that because an assistant correctly identified a qualitative problem, its quantitative claims about that same problem are equally reliable. Treating an assistant's failure to report a count-based fault (e.g. exact duplicate ids) as evidence that fault does not exist. Skipping the direct-to-file verification step because the assistant's answer sounded confident and specific.
example_code_for_ai:
# Prompt: "List every data quality problem you can find in this sheet,
# with the number of rows affected for each. Do not fix anything yet."
# Assistant reliably finds: mixed date formats, currency-as-text (visible in any sample)
# Assistant is unreliable on: "How many duplicate delivery_ids are there?"
# Real answer, verified against the file: 40 duplicated ids (not the assistant's guess)
# Rule: description from AI = useful starting point. Counts from AI = always verify.

title: Writing a Reusable Cleaning Script, in the Right Order
learning_objective: Write a pandas cleaning script that removes duplicates before other transformations, parses dates using a fixed list of known formats rather than a general parser, and standardises a currency and an identifier column.
description_for_ai: A cleaning script should run steps in a deliberate order, starting with de-duplication (drop_duplicates on the true unique key, keeping the first occurrence) before any other transformation - cleaning first and deduplicating later risks carefully repairing rows that are about to be deleted anyway. Dates should be parsed by trying a short list of explicitly named formats in a fixed order, returning nothing (not a guess) if none match; the critical property of this approach is that it never falls back to a general-purpose date parser, because a general parser silently guesses on an ambiguous format like 03-08-2026 without indicating which way it decided. A currency column stored as text (e.g. ₥45,320) is converted to a number by stripping the symbol and thousands separator before casting. An identifier column with inconsistent formatting (e.g. LAG07 vs LAG-07) is standardised with a single rule (uppercase, insert the hyphen) applied to every row, not row-by-row manual correction.
common_mistakes_for_ai: Running de-duplication after other cleaning steps instead of first, wasting effort cleaning rows that will be discarded and risking double-counting before the duplicates are removed. Using a general-purpose date parser (e.g. one that auto-detects format) instead of trying explicit named formats in order, silently misreading ambiguous dates. Converting a currency column without stripping every non-digit character first, leaving most values unconverted. Standardising an identifier column with a one-off fix for the specific values seen in this file, rather than a general pattern rule that will also work on a differently-formatted future file.
example_code_for_ai:
df = df.drop_duplicates(subset="delivery_id", keep="first")     # first, always
df["date"] = df["date"].map(parse_date)   # tries 5 named formats in order,
                                           # returns nothing if none match -
                                           # never falls back to a general parser
df["fee_naira"] = df["fee_naira"].map(money_to_int)  # strip symbol + commas
df["rider_name"] = df["rider_name"].str.strip().str.title()
df["route_code"] = df["route_code"].str.upper().str.replace(
    r"^([A-Z]{3})(\d{2})$", r"\1-\2", regex=True)

title: Deciding Which Faults to Leave as Explicit Unknowns
learning_objective: Distinguish faults that can be repaired by an explicit rule from faults that must be left as an explicit unknown rather than guessed, and apply the five-question verification checklist to a cleaning result.
description_for_ai: Some faults have no rule that can fix them honestly and must be left as an explicit unknown rather than filled in: a blank status field is not the same as a known outcome, and filling it with a guessed value (e.g. defaulting every blank to 'Delivered') invents an outcome nothing in the data supports and nothing downstream will ever be able to tell was invented; the correct handling is to leave it blank, count it explicitly, and report that count. Similarly, a date that parses successfully but falls clearly outside the valid period (e.g. a 2027 date inside a Q3 2026 file) is known to be wrong but not knowable as any specific correct value - it becomes blank/excluded, gets counted, and is flagged for the business to investigate, rather than being corrected using outside knowledge such as an answer key that would not exist in a real engagement. Once cleaning is finished, the five-question verification checklist is applied to the result: did I run it; does a number reconcile from a second, independent direction; does it hold under a filter; can every line be explained; and does the outcome make business sense.
common_mistakes_for_ai: Filling a blank field with an assumed or most-common value instead of leaving it as an explicit, counted unknown. Correcting an out-of-range value using external knowledge (such as an answer key that exists only for training purposes) rather than treating it honestly as unresolvable from the file alone. Reporting a single unknown-count figure without checking whether cleaning order (e.g. deduplication before or after) changes which specific rows are counted as unknown. Treating a passed technical verification (ran without error, totals reconcile) as sufficient without also asking whether the result makes business sense.
example_code_for_ai:
# Two faults left deliberately unfixed, not guessed:
# - 116 blank statuses in the raw sheet (115 after de-dup, since one blank
#   row is also a duplicate) -> left blank, counted, reported as "unknown"
# - Two dates outside the quarter (2027) -> excluded, counted, flagged for
#   operations to investigate, not silently corrected
# Five-question check on the cleaned result:
# 1. Did I run it? 2. Reconciles from a second direction? 3. Holds under a
# filter? 4. Can I explain every line? 5. Does it make business sense?

title: Fitting a Trend Line and Stating Its One Assumption
learning_objective: State the single assumption behind a straight-line forecast in plain language before fitting it.
description_for_ai: A straight-line trend forecast rests on exactly one assumption, and that assumption should be stated in plain language before the line is fitted: whatever has been happening over the historical window keeps happening, at the same rate, into the forecast window. This sounds trivially simple, which is exactly why it is usually left unsaid - every forecasting method has an assumption, and most of them hide it rather than state it. Making the assumption explicit up front, before looking at the fitted numbers, is what allows a forecaster to later recognise when the fitted result contradicts common sense (for example, a declining trend on a business believed to be growing) as a signal to investigate the data rather than a signal to trust the line blindly.
common_mistakes_for_ai: Fitting a trend line and reporting its result without ever stating the underlying assumption out loud, treating the method as assumption-free. Treating the trend-line assumption as unique to this method, rather than recognising every forecasting approach carries some assumption worth naming. Reporting a fitted trend's direction as fact rather than as a conclusion conditional on the stated assumption holding. Skipping a sanity check of the fitted direction against known business context before reporting it.
example_code_for_ai:
# Stated before fitting anything:
# "Whatever has been happening for the last 12 weeks keeps happening,
#  at the same rate, for the next 13 weeks."
# That single sentence is the entire assumption behind a linear trend fit.

reading R-squared and building a range

title: Partial Periods and Why They Flip a Trend's Sign
learning_objective: Identify a partial (incomplete) period at either end of a weekly time series and explain why leaving it in a trend fit can reverse the trend's apparent direction.
description_for_ai: When a data extract's date range does not align exactly with calendar week boundaries, the first and/or last grouped period in the series is partial - it holds fewer days than a typical period, so its total is naturally lower even if the underlying rate of activity has not changed. Fitting a trend line across all periods including partial ones can produce a misleadingly negative or flat slope, because the artificially low first and last values pull the line down at both ends; on the SwiftRoute Q3 data, fitting all 14 weeks (two of them partial) gave a slope of -0.347 deliveries per week with an R-squared of 0.0008 (essentially no explanatory power), while dropping the two partial weeks and refitting on the 12 complete weeks gave a slope of +2.948 deliveries per week with an R-squared of 0.3262 - the same file and method producing an opposite conclusion, purely because of which rows were included. The correct practice is to identify and exclude partial periods before fitting a trend, and this fault never announces itself with an error.
common_mistakes_for_ai: Fitting a trend line across every period in a series without first checking whether the first or last period is a partial (short) one. Concluding a business is shrinking or flat based on a trend fit that includes artificially low partial-period totals. Assuming a low-R-squared trend on the full series simply means 'no trend exists', rather than checking whether partial periods are distorting the fit. Failing to recognise that this fault produces no error or warning - the arithmetic is entirely correct for the data given to it, which is exactly what makes it dangerous.
example_code_for_ai:
# All 14 weeks (2 partial - first and last):
#   slope = -0.347/week, R-squared = 0.0008  -> looks like decline, is wrong
# 12 complete weeks only (partial weeks dropped):
#   slope = +2.948/week, R-squared = 0.3262  -> actual growth trend
# Same file, same method, opposite conclusion - only the row selection changed.

title: Reading R-Squared and Turning a Point Estimate into a Range
learning_objective: Interpret R-squared as a statement of how much variation a trend line is entitled to claim, and convert a single point forecast into a defensible range using the fit's residual error.
description_for_ai: R-squared states how much of the period-to-period variation a fitted trend line actually explains, on a scale where 1.0 would mean the line accounts for all of it. An R-squared of 0.33 (as in the SwiftRoute 12-complete-week fit) means the trend explains about a third of week-to-week movement, and the remaining two-thirds is variation the line cannot account for; this is not a pass/fail grade, but it does mean a single-figure point estimate (e.g. 'we forecast 4,049 deliveries') overstates the precision the model actually supports. The honest way to report a trend forecast is as a range built from the residuals' standard deviation: point estimate plus or minus one residual standard deviation (e.g. 4,049 with a residual standard deviation implying a range of roughly 3,840 to 4,257), paired with a plain-language statement such as 'somewhere between X and Y, most likely around Z.'
common_mistakes_for_ai: Reporting a forecast as a single precise figure (e.g. to four significant figures) without also reporting the range implied by the fit's residual error. Treating a moderate R-squared (e.g. 0.33) as evidence the model is useless, rather than recognising it as a specific, usable amount of explained variation as long as the range is reported alongside it. Treating R-squared as a grade to pass or fail rather than a statement of how much the fitted line is entitled to claim. Building the forecast range from an arbitrary margin instead of the fit's own residual standard deviation.
example_code_for_ai:
# 12-complete-week fit: slope +2.948/week, R-squared 0.3262
# Residuals: standard deviation 16.0 deliveries, MAPE 3.96%
# Honest report, not a bare point figure:
# "Point estimate 4,049; range roughly 3,840 (low) to 4,257 (high),
#  because the trend explains about a third of week-to-week movement."

title: Beating the Naive Baseline, and Using AI to Stress-Test a Forecast
learning_objective: Compare a trend forecast against a naive baseline before presenting it, and use an AI assistant to attack a forecast's assumptions rather than to generate the forecast itself.
description_for_ai: A naive baseline forecast simply holds the most recent period's average flat into the future (e.g. Q3's weekly mean projected unchanged into Q4). Any more sophisticated forecast (such as a fitted trend line) should be compared against this baseline before being presented: if the trend forecast cannot beat the naive baseline by a meaningful margin, the baseline should be reported instead, since it is simpler and equally or more accurate. On the SwiftRoute data, the trend forecast (4,049 deliveries) differed from the naive baseline (3,570) by about 480 deliveries, a difference large enough to be worth planning around, which justified using the trend method. Separately, an AI assistant is most useful for a forecast not by generating it, but by being asked to argue against it: given the fitted numbers (not the raw file), it can validly raise concerns such as thin historical data, an inability to see seasonality, or a low R-squared not supporting a precise point estimate - but it may also assert plausible-sounding claims about factors entirely outside the data (e.g. holiday-season demand spikes) that must be logged as open questions for the business, not treated as findings, since nothing in the dataset supports them.
common_mistakes_for_ai: Presenting a more complex forecasting method without first checking whether it actually beats the simple naive baseline by a meaningful margin. Using an AI assistant to produce the forecast number itself rather than to critique an already-fitted forecast's assumptions. Accepting an AI assistant's claim about a factor outside the dataset (such as a seasonal spike) as a finding, rather than recognising it as an untestable hypothesis to flag separately for the business. Failing to distinguish, when reading an AI assistant's critique, between concerns it can validly raise from the given numbers and claims it cannot actually know from those numbers.
example_code_for_ai:
# Naive baseline: Q3 weekly mean held flat = 3,570 deliveries
# Trend forecast: 4,049 deliveries (difference of ~480 - worth planning around)
# AI stress-test prompt: "I have 12 complete weeks, slope +2.95/week, R-squared
# 0.33, residual sd 16. Projected 13 weeks forward to 4,049. Argue against this
# forecast. What would make it wrong?"
# Valid critique: thin history, no visible seasonality, R-squared doesn't
# support a precise point figure. Invalid as a finding: "festive season spike"
# - no December exists in this data, so it is a question for the business.

title: Supervised Learning: Classification vs Regression
learning_objective: Explain supervised learning as learning from examples with known answers, and classify a real business prediction question as classification or regression by testing whether its output can be meaningfully ranked or subtracted.
description_for_ai: Supervised learning means training on a set of examples where the correct answer is already known for each one, so the model learns the pattern connecting inputs to that known answer. Within supervised learning, classification and regression are separated by only one question: what is being predicted, a category or a number. The reliable test is whether the possible answers can be meaningfully ranked or subtracted - 47 minutes minus 45 minutes is 2 minutes and that difference means something, making delivery duration a regression problem; 'Delivered' minus 'Returned' means nothing at all, making delivery outcome a classification problem. This test catches a common trap: an identifier or code that looks numeric (e.g. a route code like LAG-07) is still a category, because LAG-07 minus LAG-01 is not a meaningful quantity of anything, so predicting which route a delivery is assigned to is classification, not regression, despite route codes containing digits.
common_mistakes_for_ai: Classifying a prediction task as regression simply because its labels contain digits or numeric-looking codes, without testing whether subtracting two of those labels produces a meaningful result. Confusing supervised learning with any model that produces a prediction, rather than specifically meaning that historical correct answers were available to learn from. Assuming any question about 'how much' is automatically regression without checking whether the answer is actually a bounded category dressed up as a number. Treating classification and regression as different techniques rather than as different answers to the single question of what type of output is being predicted.
example_code_for_ai:
# The one test: can the answers be meaningfully ranked/subtracted?
# "Will this delivery fail?" -> Delivered/Failed/Returned/In Transit
#   -> Classification (Delivered minus Returned means nothing)
# "How many minutes will this delivery take?" -> a number, e.g. 47
#   -> Regression (47 minus 45 = 2 minutes, and that means something)
# "Which of 14 routes will a delivery be assigned to?" -> route codes
#   -> Classification, even though codes look numeric (LAG-07 minus LAG-01
#      is not six of anything)

title: Unsupervised Clustering and Where an Analyst's Job Ends
learning_objective: Explain clustering as unsupervised learning where no correct groups are supplied in advance, and state where an analyst's responsibility ends and a data scientist's begins.
description_for_ai: Clustering is unsupervised: unlike classification or regression, nobody supplies the correct groups in advance - the algorithm is handed a set of numeric features per record (e.g. delivery count, average fee, average distance per customer) and finds groups on its own, with no 'customer type' column existing anywhere in the source file to check against. The groups a clustering algorithm produces are unlabelled (e.g. group 0, 1, 2); any name given to a group afterward (such as 'frequent customers') is the analyst's own interpretation of the group's averages, not a fact the algorithm asserted, and that interpretation must be defended, not assumed. An analyst's scope in this space is clearly bounded: describing what happened and why, framing a question so it is answerable, judging whether a model's output is plausible, and communicating results to a decision maker. Building and tuning a predictive model, choosing and validating an algorithm, owning a model in production, and monitoring it for drift belong to a data scientist. Being able to state this boundary confidently, without apology, is treated as a stronger professional answer than presenting a half-built model that cannot be defended.
common_mistakes_for_ai: Treating clustering output as though the algorithm discovered a true, objective grouping rather than one candidate grouping among several equally valid ones. Presenting a clustering group's assigned name (e.g. 'frequent customers') as a fact the data asserted, rather than as the analyst's own interpretation requiring justification. Believing an analyst must be able to build and tune models to be credible, rather than recognising that knowing when to call a data scientist is itself a legitimate scope decision. Confusing an unlabelled algorithm output with a labelled business category that was already defined somewhere in the source data.
example_code_for_ai:
# Clustering: no "customer type" column exists anywhere in the file.
# Algorithm is given 3 numbers per customer (deliveries, fee, distance)
# and finds 3 groups on its own - unsupervised, because no right answer
# was ever supplied to check against.
# Analyst's job: describe, frame the question, judge plausibility, communicate.
# Data scientist's job: build/tune the model, validate it, own it in production.

title: Two Ways a Clustering Result Misleads
learning_objective: Explain how leaving clustering features on different numeric scales causes one feature to silently dominate the grouping, and explain why the number of clusters requested is an analyst decision, not a fact the data reveals.
description_for_ai: Two specific ways a clustering result can mislead, both without any error being raised. First, scaling: if input features are left on their raw, different numeric scales (e.g. a fee column running into the thousands of naira alongside a delivery-count column running from one to twelve), the distance calculation the algorithm uses becomes dominated by whichever feature has the largest raw range - in practice this meant the algorithm was effectively grouping customers by fee alone while appearing to have considered every feature, and only about 74% of customers landed in the same group as the properly scaled version, with nothing in the output warning that this had happened. Second, the number of groups (k) requested is a choice the analyst makes and must defend, not something the data hands over as fact: re-running the same clustering asking for five groups instead of three produces an equally confident, equally 'valid-looking' but different answer, and a clustering result presented without justification for why that specific number of groups was chosen has not actually been shown as a finding.
common_mistakes_for_ai: Running a clustering algorithm on features with very different raw numeric scales without first standardising or scaling them, allowing the largest-range feature to dominate the result unnoticed. Treating a clustering result as objectively correct because it 'ran without error', when scaling and cluster-count choices can both silently produce a misleading grouping. Assuming the number of clusters is something the algorithm determines, rather than a parameter the analyst chose and must justify. Presenting a clustering result to a decision maker without being able to explain why that specific number of groups was requested.
example_code_for_ai:
# Fault 1 - unscaled features:
# fee ~ thousands of naira; deliveries ~ 1-12  -> distance calc dominated by
# fee alone. Only 74% of customers land in the same group vs the properly
# scaled version, with no warning.
# Fault 2 - arbitrary k:
# Re-run asking for 5 groups instead of 3 -> equally confident, different
# answer. The group count is an analyst decision to defend, not a fact found.

title: Deciding What Is Automatable: Rules vs Judgement
learning_objective: Split a recurring reporting task into its individual steps and classify each as automatable (a rule) or not automatable (a judgement call).
description_for_ai: Before automating any recurring task, it should be split into its individual steps, each classified as either a rule (automatable) or a judgement (not automatable). Rule-based steps include removing duplicate records by a known key, parsing dates in known formats, standardising codes by a known pattern, and totalling values by a known grouping - each of these applies the same logic every time regardless of which specific numbers appear. Judgement-based steps include deciding whether an unusual result is a genuine data fault or a real business event, and writing the sentence that tells a stakeholder what to do about a finding - these require reasoning about context that changes each time and cannot be reduced to a fixed rule. The line falls in the same place every time this exercise is done: if a step is automated that is actually a judgement, the analyst has not saved time, they have hidden a decision inside code where nobody will notice it was made.
common_mistakes_for_ai: Automating a step that actually requires judgement (such as deciding whether an anomaly is a data fault or a real event) because it looks procedural on the surface. Leaving a genuinely rule-based, repetitive step (such as parsing known date formats) as manual work indefinitely, wasting time that automation would safely reclaim. Treating 'this step is boring/repetitive' as the criterion for automating it, rather than 'this step is the same rule every time'. Failing to recognise that automating a judgement step doesn't remove the decision, it just hides who made it and when.
example_code_for_ai:
# Step-by-step classification of a recurring SwiftRoute quarterly report:
# Remove duplicate delivery ids           -> Automatable (a rule)
# Parse dates in known formats             -> Automatable (formats are known)
# Standardise route codes before joining   -> Automatable (a known pattern)
# Total deliveries/revenue by month        -> Automatable
# Decide if an unusual month is a fault or a real event -> NOT automatable
# Write the sentence telling Adaeze what to do           -> NOT automatable
not_yet_taught: the four rules for a refresh-proof automation

title: The Four Rules for an Automation That Survives a Refresh
learning_objective: State and apply the four rules that determine whether a report automation still works correctly after the underlying data changes.
description_for_ai: Four rules, each one existing because an automation broke on exactly that point in real practice: (1) the file path must be an argument the script receives, never a constant hardcoded inside it, because a path buried in the code means someone has to edit code just to run a routine report; (2) reporting periods (e.g. month names) must be derived from the data itself, never hardcoded as a fixed list, because a hardcoded list of periods has an expiry date the moment the next period arrives; (3) identifier or code columns must be standardised before they are joined, never after, because two differently formatted versions of the same code (e.g. LAG07 and LAG-07) will silently fail to match in a join and drop rows with no warning; (4) an automation must assert what it expects (row counts, totals, coverage) so that when reality stops matching the assumption, it fails loudly with a clear message rather than publishing a confidently wrong report.
common_mistakes_for_ai: Hardcoding a file path directly inside a script instead of accepting it as an argument or parameter. Hardcoding a list of expected periods (e.g. specific month names) instead of deriving the reporting window from the data's actual date range. Standardising identifier formats after a join has already been performed instead of before, silently losing unmatched rows. Writing an automation with no internal assertions or checks, so that a broken assumption produces a wrong report with no failure signal at all.
example_code_for_ai:
# Four rules, each with the failure it prevents:
# 1. File path as an argument, never a constant       -> avoids editing code to run
# 2. Periods derived from the data, never hardcoded    -> avoids an expiry date
# 3. Standardise codes BEFORE joining, never after     -> avoids silent join drops
# 4. Assert expected counts/totals                     -> fails loudly, not quietly wrong
def run_report(file_path):
    assert file_path is not None  # rule 1: caller supplies the path

title: Building a Parameterised Report Script with AI Assistance
learning_objective: Write a Python function, with an AI assistant drafting the routine parts, that reads a delivery export as a file-path argument, cleans it by known rules, and reports periods derived from the data.
description_for_ai: A parameterised report script accepts the file path as a function argument rather than a hardcoded value, then applies the same rule-based cleaning established for the raw data: remove duplicate delivery ids keeping the first occurrence, parse dates using a fixed set of known formats (never a general-purpose parser, since a general parser resolves an ambiguous format like 03-08-2026 silently and without indicating which way it decided), convert a currency column stored as text into a number, and standardise identifier codes into one consistent pattern. An AI assistant is useful for drafting this boilerplate quickly when given a precise specification (the exact formats, the exact transformation rules) - the division of labour that works is the assistant writing the routine parts fast while the analyst owns every rule that decides what the numbers actually mean, including explicitly rejecting a general date parser if the assistant defaults to one.
common_mistakes_for_ai: Accepting an AI-drafted date-parsing function that uses a general-purpose parser without checking whether it silently resolves ambiguous formats. Hardcoding the file path or period list inside the AI-drafted function instead of keeping them as arguments or data-derived values. Running an AI-generated script without reading it line by line first to confirm each rule matches the specification given. Treating the AI-drafted script as finished once it runs without error, without checking its output against expected counts and totals.
example_code_for_ai:
def build_report(file_path):
    df = pd.read_excel(file_path, sheet_name="deliveries")
    df = df.drop_duplicates(subset="delivery_id", keep="first")
    df["date"] = df["date"].map(parse_known_formats)   # 5 named formats, in order
    df["fee_naira"] = df["fee_naira"].map(money_to_int)
    df["route_code"] = standardise_route_code(df["route_code"])
    periods = sorted(df["date"].dt.to_period("M").dropna().unique())  # from data
    return df, periods

title: Proving an Automation Survives a Refresh with a Test
learning_objective: Write a test that manufactures a plausible next-period file with realistic changes and asserts the automation's report still behaves correctly against it.
description_for_ai: An automation's claim to be reliable must be proven, not asserted from confidence. A refresh test manufactures a plausible next-period version of the input file, deliberately changing everything a real data refresh would change: every date shifted forward, a brand-new category value introduced that never appeared before (e.g. a new route code), a subset of existing rows re-formatted differently (e.g. an identifier missing its usual hyphen), some rows removed so no total can be trivially reused, and column order shuffled since real exports do this routinely. The test then runs the automation against both the original and the manufactured file and asserts specific properties: that reporting periods followed the new data rather than a stale constant, that the brand-new category value reached the report output, that no incorrectly formatted identifier survived the cleaning and join, and that totals were freshly recomputed rather than carried over from the previous run. Passing every one of these checks, not the developer's confidence, is what makes an automation safe to hand over for unattended future use.
common_mistakes_for_ai: Testing an automation only against the exact file it was built on, never against a file with realistic changes (new categories, shifted dates, different formatting, removed rows, reordered columns). Writing a test that checks the script runs without crashing but does not assert specific expected values, missing cases where the script runs cleanly but produces a wrong result. Assuming a script that worked correctly once on the original file will continue to work correctly indefinitely, without a repeatable test to re-run after future changes. Building test data that changes too little (e.g. only new dates) to actually exercise rules 2, 3, and 4 from the automation's design.
example_code_for_ai:
# test_refresh.py builds a manufactured "next quarter" file:
# - every date shifted forward one quarter
# - a brand-new route code appears (never seen before)
# - some existing rows arrive with an unhyphenated identifier variant
# - some rows removed (so no total can be reused/copied)
# - column order shuffled
# Then asserts, among other checks:
assert new_route_code in report.routes          # new category reached the report
assert unhyphenated_variant not in report.routes  # cleaning/join held up
assert report.total != previous_report.total      # recomputed, not carried over

title: Four Ways AI Output Fails in Analysis
learning_objective: Name and distinguish four distinct ways AI-assisted analysis output can be wrong: hallucinated values, plausible wrong code, silent assumption changes, and correct arithmetic answering the wrong question.
description_for_ai: Four distinct failure modes recur across AI-assisted analysis work. Hallucinated values: a figure stated fluently and confidently that is not actually present in or derivable from the data (e.g. an assistant answering a count question it never actually scanned the file to compute). Plausible wrong code: code that runs without error, returns no warning, and computes something other than what was intended (e.g. a reporting window derived from min/max date that silently absorbed two out-of-range rows, changing a three-month report into a five-month one). Silent assumption changes: a decision made by a tool or method without being surfaced or agreed to (e.g. a general date parser resolving an ambiguous date one specific way without indicating that a choice was even made). Correct arithmetic, wrong question: every individual calculation is right, every technical check passes, and the overall conclusion is still nonsense, because the numbers being combined were never actually comparable in the first place. The first three are technical failures that careful coding and testing can catch; the fourth is not a coding failure at all, and it is the one that survives every technical safeguard.
common_mistakes_for_ai: Treating all AI-related errors as the same category of mistake, rather than recognising they require different detection strategies (checking source data, testing code, questioning defaults, and questioning the comparison itself). Assuming that because code ran without error and returned a plausible number, none of the four failure modes are present. Believing the fourth failure mode (correct arithmetic, wrong question) will be caught by the same technical checks (does it run, does it reconcile) that catch the first three. Only watching for these failure modes in AI-generated work, rather than recognising a human analyst can produce the same four failure modes unassisted.
example_code_for_ai:
# Four failure modes, each with its own example from this module:
# 1. Hallucinated values   - assistant guessed a duplicate-id count before scanning
# 2. Plausible wrong code  - report window silently absorbed 2 out-of-range dates
# 3. Silent assumption change - general date parser resolved 03-08-2026 unasked
# 4. Correct arithmetic, wrong question - the margin-by-route comparison (Part 3)
not_yet_taught: assembling the checklist and prompt log

title: The Five-Question Verification Checklist
learning_objective: Apply the five-question verification checklist to a finished analysis deliverable, and explain why the fifth question is the only one that catches a result that is technically correct but doesn't make sense.
description_for_ai: The five-question verification checklist, applied to any finished analysis output: (1) Did I run it? - the output must come from an actual execution, not an assumption of what it would produce. (2) Does one number reconcile from a second, independent direction? - every total has an independent check (a sum has a count, a rate has its own numerator and denominator, a join has a predictable row count). (3) Does it hold under a filter? - a result checked only at the aggregate level can hide a fault that only appears in a subset. (4) Can I explain every line? - if a step in the process cannot be narrated and justified, it should not be trusted. (5) Does the answer make business sense? - the only non-technical question of the five, and the only one capable of catching a result where every technical check passes and the conclusion is still nonsense, because it asks whether a domain expert would actually object to the finding.
common_mistakes_for_ai: Treating the five questions as a formality to complete after the fact rather than a genuine check that can change the reported conclusion. Skipping question five because the first four all passed, missing the one failure mode that specifically survives technical checks. Answering question five with a simple yes without asking who specifically would object and why, which produces a superficial pass rather than a genuine check. Being unable to name a specific second, independent direction for question two, which means the number was re-read rather than actually verified.
example_code_for_ai:
# The five questions, applied to any finished output:
# 1. Did I run it?
# 2. Does one number reconcile from a second direction?
# 3. Does it hold under a filter?
# 4. Can I explain every line?
# 5. Does the answer make business sense?
# Q5 is the only non-technical question, and the only one that catches
# a result that passes 1-4 and is still nonsense.

title: Correct Arithmetic, Wrong Question: the Mismatched-Grain Trap
learning_objective: Diagnose a result where every calculation and technical check passes but the conclusion is implausible, by identifying that the two data sources being compared are not at the same grain.
description_for_ai: A comparison can pass every technical verification question (it ran, a number reconciles from a second direction, it holds under a filter, every line can be explained) and still produce a nonsensical conclusion, because the underlying data sources being combined were never actually comparable. In the SwiftRoute case, a route-level margin was computed as delivery revenue minus fuel cost per route, and the result showed every one of 14 routes losing money, with fuel cost roughly double delivery revenue for the quarter - each individual sheet was independently sound (the fuel efficiency and per-litre price were both realistic for a Nigerian van fleet, and the mean delivery fee was realistic for the distances involved), but the fuel sheet was a fleet-level bill while the delivery sheet was a partial extract of roughly three deliveries per route per day, so the two were not at the same grain and could not be meaningfully subtracted from each other. The correct deliverable in this situation is not the (wrong) headline finding ('every route loses money'); it is the honest statement that the two data sources cannot be compared until someone clarifies what the delivery extract is a sample of - that clarifying question is itself worth more than the numeric result.
common_mistakes_for_ai: Reporting a comparison's numeric result as a finding once the first four verification questions pass, without checking whether the two data sources involved are actually at the same grain. Assuming that because each individual data source looks internally realistic, a calculation combining them must also be valid. Blaming one of the two data sources as 'wrong' when a comparison produces an implausible result, rather than questioning whether the comparison itself was ever valid. Treating a comparison that fails only question five ('does this make business sense') as merely surprising rather than as evidence the underlying data was mismatched.
example_code_for_ai:
# Route margin = delivery revenue (from a ~3,600-row extract) minus
# fuel cost (a fleet-level bill) -> 14 of 14 routes show negative margin,
# fuel cost roughly double revenue for the quarter.
# Each sheet alone is realistic (km/litre, price/litre, fee/distance all sane).
# The fault: the two sheets are not at the same grain - a fleet bill vs a
# partial per-route extract - so subtracting one from the other is invalid.
# Correct deliverable: "these two sheets cannot be compared until the
# extract's sampling basis is clarified" - not "every route is loss-making".

title: Assembling the Verification Checklist and Prompt Log for Submission
learning_objective: Assemble a completed five-question verification checklist with one line of evidence per question, alongside a prompt log documenting what was asked of an AI assistant and what was changed before using its answer.
description_for_ai: Every AI-assisted deliverable is submitted with two accompanying artefacts: a completed verification checklist, with one specific line of evidence against each of the five questions (not a bare yes/no), and a prompt log listing what was asked of the AI assistant at each step and what was changed about its answer before it was used. A prompt log entry describing a prompt that produced a wrong or incomplete answer, which was then caught and corrected, is more valuable evidence than a log of only successful prompts, because it demonstrates active checking rather than passive acceptance. A prompt log entry where nothing was changed about the AI's answer before using it is itself worth flagging explicitly, since it invites the reviewer to check that verification genuinely happened rather than being skipped.
common_mistakes_for_ai: Submitting a verification checklist with a bare yes/no per question instead of one specific line of evidence per question. Including only prompts that produced correct, unmodified answers in the prompt log, omitting the prompts that had to be corrected. Treating the prompt log as a formality rather than as evidence that verification actually took place at each step. Leaving an entry where nothing was changed from the AI's answer unflagged, rather than noting it so a reviewer can check it was genuinely verified rather than skipped.
example_code_for_ai:
# Verification checklist entry (not bare yes/no):
# Q2: "Fee total reconciled against a separate sum of the raw column after
#      stripping currency symbols - matched to the naira."
# Prompt log entry (a corrected one, the most valuable kind):
# "Asked for a date parser; it defaulted to a general parser. Rejected it
#  and specified the 5 named formats explicitly instead."
